simpleExplanation: The price-to-earnings ratio compares a share's price with the profit earned for each share.
whyItMatters: It offers a quick way to see how much investors are paying for a company's current earnings.
example: A share priced at ₹200 with EPS of ₹10 has a P/E ratio of 20.
beginnerTakeaway: A high or low P/E is not automatically good or bad; compare similar companies and consider growth and risk.

simpleExplanation: Earnings per share is the company's profit divided across its outstanding shares.
whyItMatters: It shows how much profit belongs to each share and is used in several valuation measures.
example: If a company earns ₹100 crore and has 10 crore shares, its EPS is ₹10.
beginnerTakeaway: Look for consistent EPS growth, but check whether it comes from the core business.

simpleExplanation: Return on equity measures how efficiently a company uses shareholders' money to generate profit.
whyItMatters: It helps compare management efficiency among companies in the same sector.
example: A company earning ₹20 crore on ₹100 crore of shareholder equity has 20% ROE.
beginnerTakeaway: Strong ROE is more useful when it is consistent and not driven by excessive debt.

simpleExplanation: Return on capital employed measures profit generated from both equity and long-term debt used by the business.
whyItMatters: It is useful for understanding efficiency in businesses that need a lot of capital.
example: If operating profit is ₹18 crore on ₹120 crore of capital employed, ROCE is 15%.
beginnerTakeaway: Compare ROCE with peers and the company's own history rather than reading it alone.

simpleExplanation: This ratio compares money borrowed by a company with money invested by its shareholders.
whyItMatters: More debt can increase growth in good times but also raises repayment pressure when business slows.
example: Debt of ₹50 crore and equity of ₹100 crore gives a debt-to-equity ratio of 0.5.
beginnerTakeaway: Acceptable debt levels vary by sector, so compare like with like.

simpleExplanation: Market capitalization is the total market value of all a company's shares.
whyItMatters: It indicates company size and can help set expectations about stability and growth.
example: Ten crore shares priced at ₹500 each create a market capitalization of ₹5,000 crore.
beginnerTakeaway: Share price alone does not tell you whether a company is large or small.

simpleExplanation: Revenue is the money a company earns from selling goods or services before expenses are deducted.
whyItMatters: Growing revenue can show increasing demand, but it does not guarantee profit.
example: Selling one lakh subscriptions at ₹500 each produces revenue of ₹5 crore.
beginnerTakeaway: Check whether revenue growth is steady and whether profit grows with it.

simpleExplanation: Net profit is what remains after operating costs, interest, taxes, and other expenses are paid.
whyItMatters: It shows the final earnings available to the company and its shareholders.
example: Revenue of ₹100 crore minus total expenses of ₹88 crore leaves ₹12 crore of net profit.
beginnerTakeaway: Read the notes to check whether profit includes a one-time gain.

simpleExplanation: Profit margin shows what percentage of revenue becomes profit.
whyItMatters: It reveals how well a company controls costs and converts sales into earnings.
example: A ₹10 crore profit on ₹100 crore of revenue equals a 10% profit margin.
beginnerTakeaway: Compare margins within the same industry and watch their direction over time.

simpleExplanation: Dividend yield compares annual cash dividends per share with the share's market price.
whyItMatters: It helps investors understand the cash income a share may provide relative to its price.
example: A ₹5 annual dividend on a ₹250 share gives a 2% dividend yield.
beginnerTakeaway: A very high yield can be temporary or signal stress; check whether the dividend is sustainable.

simpleExplanation: Beta estimates how strongly a share tends to move compared with the overall market.
whyItMatters: It provides one view of market-related risk, though it cannot predict future moves.
example: A beta of 1.3 suggests the share has historically moved more sharply than the market.
beginnerTakeaway: Beta describes past relative movement, not the chance of permanent loss.

simpleExplanation: Volatility describes how widely and frequently an investment's price moves.
whyItMatters: Larger swings can make an investment harder to hold and may not suit a short time horizon.
example: A share moving between ₹80 and ₹120 may be more volatile than one staying between ₹98 and ₹102.
beginnerTakeaway: Price movement is only one kind of risk; also study the business and your time horizon.

simpleExplanation: Compound annual growth rate is the steady yearly rate that would connect a starting value to an ending value.
whyItMatters: It makes multi-year growth easier to compare, even when actual yearly returns varied.
example: Growing from ₹100 to about ₹161 over five years is roughly a 10% CAGR.
beginnerTakeaway: CAGR smooths the journey, so also look at the year-by-year changes.

simpleExplanation: Liquidity is how easily an investment can be bought or sold without causing a large price change.
whyItMatters: Low liquidity can make it harder or more expensive to exit when needed.
example: A widely traded large-company share is usually more liquid than a rarely traded small-company share.
beginnerTakeaway: Check trading activity before assuming you can sell quickly at the displayed price.

simpleExplanation: Diversification means spreading money across different investments instead of relying on one.
whyItMatters: Poor performance in one holding may have less impact when other holdings behave differently.
example: Owning businesses across banking, technology, healthcare, and consumer goods is more diversified than owning only banks.
beginnerTakeaway: Diversification can reduce concentration risk, but it cannot remove all market risk.

simpleExplanation: A bull market is an extended period when prices broadly rise and investor confidence is strong.
whyItMatters: Optimism can lift many assets and make risky decisions feel safer than they are.
example: A broad index rising over many months while participation expands may be described as a bull market.
beginnerTakeaway: Rising prices do not replace research or make valuation irrelevant.

simpleExplanation: A bear market is a sustained period of broad price declines and weak investor confidence.
whyItMatters: Falling markets test risk tolerance and can expose weak businesses or excessive debt.
example: A broad index falling substantially from its recent high over several months may be called a bear market.
beginnerTakeaway: A market decline is not automatically a reason to panic; revisit your goals, horizon, and facts.

simpleExplanation: Intrinsic value is an estimate of what an investment is worth based on its future cash generation and risks.
whyItMatters: It encourages investors to separate business value from the price currently quoted by the market.
example: Two analysts can use different growth assumptions and reach different intrinsic value estimates for the same company.
beginnerTakeaway: Intrinsic value is an estimate, not a guaranteed correct price.

simpleExplanation: A balance sheet lists what a company owns, what it owes, and the shareholders' remaining interest at a point in time.
whyItMatters: It helps reveal debt, cash reserves, working capital, and overall financial strength.
example: Assets of ₹150 crore minus liabilities of ₹90 crore leave shareholder equity of ₹60 crore.
beginnerTakeaway: Look at how assets, debt, and cash change across several reporting periods.

simpleExplanation: Cash flow tracks actual cash entering and leaving a business through operations, investing, and financing.
whyItMatters: A company can report accounting profit while struggling to collect cash.
example: A profitable company may have weak operating cash flow if customers have not yet paid their bills.
beginnerTakeaway: Healthy profit is more convincing when operating cash flow supports it over time.
